target_description: Conditional backtest of UK Corporation Tax receipts R_{y+1} (£bn nominal, ONS N445 central-government CT gross of tax credits, `D-ons-ct-receipts` / `D-obr-databank`) predicted from information at fiscal year y-1, conditioning on realised 2-year profit growth (`pnfc_gos`, `D-ons-pnfc-gos`) from y-1 to y+1 (note: the forward engine baseline uses OBR onshore CT receipts, a different receipt perimeter). This conditional design isolates tax-policy response modelling from macroeconomic forecast error. Chronological split: train on FY <= 2007, out-of-sample test on FY >= 2008 (FY2008-09 to FY2024-25). Leave-one-out 90% (5th–95th percentile) empirical residual interval coverage on FY2008-09 to FY2024-25: 15/17 (88.2%).

methods.label: Naive profit-growth baseline
methods.description: R̂_{y+1} = R_{y-1} × (1 + g_{y-1→y+1}), assuming receipts grow one-for-one with the profit proxy and ignoring tax-rate changes.

methods.label: Static tax-rate scaling baseline
methods.description: R̂_{y+1} = naive × (s·t_new/t_old + (1−s)), scaling the main-rate share s of receipts proportionally to the statutory rate change with zero behavioural response.

methods.label: Jane Avenue behavioural engine (central prior ε)
methods.description: Engine static + behavioural revenue equation with central taxable-profit elasticity ε = 0.20 and main-rate profit share s = 0.85.

methods.label: Jane Avenue behavioural engine (train-calibrated ε; bound hit)
methods.description: Same structural revenue equation with elasticity ε reached the search bound of 1.500 on [0.0, 1.5] (corner solution; not identified on FY ≤ 2007 training data because the 1984–86 rate cuts coincided with capital-allowance base-broadening). Out-of-sample MAE is statistically indistinguishable from the central prior on n = 17; not exposed as an engine parameter.

methods.label: Log-change OLS baseline

ml_experiment.conclusion: NOT ADOPTED: LightGBM achieved an out-of-sample test MAE of £6.33bn on FY2008-09–FY2024-25, which fails to beat the best simple baseline `static` (test MAE £5.65bn) and the structural engine `jane_behavioural` (test MAE £5.48bn), despite a much lower in-sample train MAE of £3.27bn on FY1983-84–FY2007-08. Three structural factors explain this train/test gap: (1) tiny annual sample size (n=24 training observations), (2) regime shift between the training era (30–50% CT rates, higher Bank Rate) and the post-2008 test era (19–28% CT rates, near-zero interest rates, and the 2023 rate hike from 19% to 25%), and (3) tree models' piecewise-constant leaves cannot extrapolate log-growth responses outside the training feature support. Per product rules, ML is rejected and not wired into the live simulator.

research_eval.notes: Evaluated 15 gold factual UK CT questions (15/15 facts accurate, 15/15 source URLs HTTP-verified, 15/15 quotes verified verbatim, 0 hallucinated sources, 15/15 Tier-1 official sources).

verification_eval.notes: Clean case: approved; flagged checks: none.

limitations: Conditional backtest design: predictions of R_{y+1} condition on realised 2-year profit growth from y-1 to y+1 (measured via `pnfc_gos`). This isolates tax-rate response modelling from macroeconomic forecast error, so out-of-sample errors in unconditional real-time forecasting would be larger.

Small sample of policy regime shifts: UK corporation tax main-rate history since FY1982 contains only 16 implemented statutory rate changes (8 in the FY <= 2007 training split and 8 in the FY >= 2008 test split).

Simultaneous base-broadening and relief confounders: major rate changes coincided with structural base changes—most notably the 1983–1986 phased rate cuts paired with first-year capital-allowance abolition, and the April 2023 rise (19% -> 25%) paired with full expensing for plant & machinery and the 19% small profits rate / marginal relief.

Train-calibrated elasticity corner solution: fitting ε by nonlinear least squares on FY <= 2007 reached the search bound of 1.500 on [0.0, 1.5] (not identified on FY <= 2007 data because the 1984–86 cuts came with capital-allowance base-broadening, so a large ε mostly absorbs the base changes). Its out-of-sample MAE on n = 17 test years is statistically indistinguishable from the central prior (ε = 0.20), so it is not exposed as an alternative engine parameter.

Official costings are not ground truth and may reflect multi-year joint packages: `official_costing_gbp_bn` reports ex-ante HMT/OBR policy costings (revenue delta relative to a contemporary Budget baseline under ex-ante macro assumptions), whereas `observed` and model `predictions` are total fiscal-year CT receipts R_{y+1} (£bn). In particular, `CT-MAIN-2012` (-£0.73bn for FY2013-14, `D-budget2012`) and `CT-MAIN-2013` (-£0.82bn for FY2014-15, `D-budget2012`) are from the same Budget 2012 joint phased package, and `CT-MAIN-2017` (-£1.60bn for FY2018-19, `D-budget2015`) is from the Summer Budget 2015 joint 2017/2020 package—not isolated single-step estimates.

Receipt perimeter and baseline difference (`D-ons-ct-receipts` vs `D-obr-databank`): historical backtest `ct_receipts` is ONS series N445 central-government Corporation Tax receipts gross of tax credits (and `pnfc_gos` is the ONS `D-ons-pnfc-gos` private non-financial corporations gross operating surplus proxy), whereas the forward simulation engine baseline (`D-obr-databank`) uses OBR onshore Corporation Tax receipts. Historical backtest errors on N445 combine onshore/offshore regimes, Quarterly Instalment Payments (QIPs) timing transitions, bank surcharge, and tax-credit grossing, and therefore differ in perimeter from the engine's onshore baseline target.

OLS of log((receipts/t)/pnfc_gos) on log(1-t) over n=44 fiscal years (controlling for real GDP growth) yields an implied base elasticity of 2.642 (SE 0.185), compared with the engine central prior of 0.20. Because UK rate cuts in the 1980s and 2010s coincided with base-broadening capital-allowance reforms and post-2008 financial-sector profit shifts, macro time-series regressions confound rate effects with base definitions; we retain the micro-econometric literature prior (0.20) as central.
